extracted.intended_audience: lawmakers, regulatory attorneys, policy analysts, scholars, and interested members of the public concerned with administrative law and the Congressional Review Act
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory guidance on the Congressional Review Act (CRA): how the statute operates, key statutory requirements and precedents, strategic/policy implications, and related legislative proposals (e.g., REINS Act) for reviewing or disapproving agency rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission requirement for CRA effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRA stipulates that rules do not go into effect until after they have been submitted to Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many rules historically were not submitted to Congress, some scholars and litigants (e.g., Pacific Legal Foundation) have argued those rules may not actually be in effect and therefore could be subject to CRA repeal. The page describes three suggested ways to address previously unsubmitted rules: (1) the White House could submit the rule now and then Congress could repeal it under the CRA; (2) the White House could publish notice that a rule not in effect is being withdrawn or abandoned; or (3) a court could hold the rule invalid on the ground that it was never in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether guidance qualifies as a 'rule' (triggering the CRA window)
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination that a guidance document or other agency action 'rises to the significance of being a rule' will start the 60‑day CRA window and make the action subject to potential disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO legal opinions and other official determinations can be used to classify guidance as a 'rule' for CRA purposes (example: GAO's December 5, 2017 opinion that a 2013 CFPB auto-lending guidance qualified as a 'rule', which launched the 60‑day window according to the Senate parliamentarian). The page notes that this line-drawing has been central to efforts (e.g., S.J. Res. 57) to expand CRA use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on issuing 'substantially similar' rules after CRA repeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRA prohibits any regulation being issued that is 'substantially similar' to one already repealed under the CRA, unless Congress explicitly authorizes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibition has been identified as enabling a preemptive/regulatory strategy: an administration could issue a liberal regulation and have it repealed under the CRA to block future administrations from issuing substantially similar regulations without explicit congressional approval. The page discusses this as a possible avenue for expanding CRA power and notes attendant concerns about creating legal uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: REINS Act 'major rule' definition criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The REINS Act (proposed) would define a 'major rule' as one that would likely meet one or more specified thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill's proposed definition lists three prongs: a rule that would likely (1) affect the economy by $100 million or more a year; (2) cause a major increase in costs or prices for consumers, industries, government, or regions; or (3) significantly affect competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or the ability of U.S. businesses to compete with foreign competitors. These numeric and qualitative thresholds are the statutory criteria contemplated by REINS for labeling a rule 'major.'

rubrics_metrics.name: REINS Act congressional-approval procedure for major rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the REINS Act proposals, no proposed major rule could take effect unless Congress affirmatively approved it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes the procedural consequence: establishing a congressional approval process for all major rules so that affirmative congressional action would be required before a major rule could take effect. It also notes the legislative history — multiple House passages across Congresses and repeated Senate failures — and procedural obstacles (e.g., Byrd Rule issues in reconciliation).

rubrics_metrics.name: CRA as an avenue that avoids the Senate 60‑vote cloture requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRA provides one of the few Senate procedures that can be used to disapprove rules without invoking the ordinary 60‑vote cloture threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this feature the CRA became politically attractive (for example in the 115th Congress) and encouraged novel theories for expanding the CRA's reach. The page frames this as a strategic/structural property of the statute that informs how lawmakers consider using it.

rubrics_metrics.name: GAO and Senate-parliamentarian precedents influence CRA application
rubrics_metrics.description: GAO legal opinions and Senate precedent/parliamentarian rulings are central to interpreting when and how the CRA applies (e.g., whether an action is a 'rule', timing for the 60‑day window, and exemptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites numerous GAO decisions and Senate precedents (e.g., GAO confirmations that certain agency actions qualify as rules for CRA purposes; the Senate parliamentarian's role in determining when the 60‑day window is triggered and whether certain waivers are subject to CRA). Examples include GAO opinions on BLM plans and the GAO/Parliamentarian determinations relating to CFPB guidance and California vehicle waivers. These precedents materially affect whether CRA disapproval is procedurally available.
